MULTIFAN-CL to opal: south-west Pacific albacore

Bridging the 2024 WCPFC south Pacific albacore diagnostic model, a two-region MULTIFAN-CL model, to a single-region opal model

Author

Nicholas Ducharme-Barth

Published

November 5, 2026

Setup: read the caches 
# Code is shown (folded) in the HTML version and hidden in the PDF.

1 Overview

This document converts the 2024 stock assessment of south Pacific albacore (Thunnus alalunga) (Teears et al. 2024), a two-region MULTIFAN-CL (MFCL, Fournier et al. 1998; Davies et al. 2025) model, into opal, an RTMB age-structured model with one region. Any model runs here are preliminary explorations and should not be used as is for management advice. opal is not changed: where it cannot represent the MFCL model, the MFCL model is simplified (in MFCL) or the difference is measured with replays (standalone simulations) and documented. The comparisons are meant as advice to opal’s developers on the features the stock would need.

  • An MFCL bridge to model region 1 (Section 3). Five steps, each a refitted MFCL model: the diagnostic model (M0), no movement (M1), the movement weeks moved onto fishing dates (M1b), region 1 only (M2), and growth fixed without the conditional age-at-length data (M3). Region 1’s spawning biomass roughly doubles at each step: the stock’s scale is weakly determined, and each source of information removed lets it drift up.
  • The conversion (Section 4) maps MFCL’s October-September model year, its quarterly and monthly fishing incidents, the indices and the length compositions onto opal with four seasons, and takes biology at age from MFCL.
  • At MFCL’s values opal reproduces MFCL (Section 5): its initial numbers and recruitment exactly, its spawning biomass within 2.1%. Replays put the gap on catch timing (start-of-quarter removal against MFCL’s Baranov removal at each incident’s date); seasonal selectivity hardly matters for spawning biomass.
  • The fits (Section 6). With MFCL’s selectivity fixed, opal’s scale is unbounded (O1): the length compositions keep improving towards an unexploited stock. The cause (Section 7) is length-at-age timing: MFCL predicts each length sample at its date with lengths that grow through the year, opal from start-of-year length-at-age. With opal’s growth at MFCL’s mid-year lengths (O1-mid) the fit is bounded, with B0 at MFCL’s Beverton-Holt B0; opal’s stock is still about half MFCL’s in 2022, because MFCL starts far above its own unfished equilibrium (Section 7.1). Estimating the initial population (O1i) brings it close to MFCL’s. With opal’s own selectivity (Section 9) the double normals collapse to knife-edges and the stock is a quarter of MFCL’s.
  • Seasonal set-ups (Section 8). Splitting the fisheries with seasonal selectivity into one fishery per season, and an opal model with quarterly age classes and time steps (recruitment kept annual), are set up through opal’s inputs alone.
  • What opal would need is summarised in Section 10.

2 The 2024 assessment

The assessment (Teears et al. 2024) covers the south Pacific from the equator to 50°S and from 140°E to the coast of South America, in two regions: region 1 is the southern WCPFC Convention Area, including the overlap area with the EPO, and region 2 the rest of the EPO. Fisheries are defined as areas-as-fleets within each region (six areas in region 1, three in region 2).

  • Time. 1954 to the third quarter of 2022. The model year runs October-September with recruitment on 1 October (week 37 of the calendar year in the report), 12 annual age classes (the last a plus group); catches are taken by quarter (longline, driftnet) or month (troll).
  • Fisheries. 17 extraction fisheries (13 in region 1: longline by flag group and area, two troll fisheries and a driftnet fishery; 4 in region 2) and three index fisheries (region 1: longline north of 25°S and New Zealand troll; region 2: longline). Catches are in numbers except troll and driftnet (weight). The catch-conditioned approach solves the Baranov catch equation for fishing mortality at each fishing incident.
  • Indices. sdmTMB standardised CPUE (Anderson et al. 2022) with time-varying CVs; the troll index’s generic CV is set to 0.2.
  • Length compositions. 50 2-cm bins from 30 cm, re-weighted by catch; robust normal likelihood; sample sizes capped at 1000 and divided by Francis (2011) weights; samples below 50 fish dropped.
  • Conditional age-at-length. 654 otolith ages in 33 fishery-quarter strata, effective sample size 0.75 of the observed.
  • Biology. von Bertalanffy growth with offsets at ages 2-4 (L1 fixed at 45.5 cm); M-at-age inversely proportional to length (Lorenzen 1996), scaled to average 0.36 over ages 4-12; spawning potential from maturity and sex ratio at length; Beverton-Holt steepness 0.8 with a weak penalty (CV 0.71) on recruitment deviations; fixed recruitment distribution (0.819 in region 1) and movement from SEAPODYM (Senina et al. 2020).
  • Selectivity. Length-based cubic splines (3-4 nodes), grouped across fisheries (16 groups), seasonal (four seasons) for the tropical longline fisheries 1-7 and the EPO fishery 14, non-decreasing for the longline indices.

The assessment found the stock not overfished and not subject to overfishing (median SBrecent/SBF=0 0.48 across the model ensemble, including estimation uncertainty).

3 The MFCL bridge

Code 
B = merge(L, TS[year == min(year), .(step, sb_1954 = sb / 1000)], by = "step")
B = merge(B, TS[year == max(year), .(step, sb_2022 = sb / 1000, depletion)], by = "step")
knitr::kable(B[, .(step, objective = fmt(objective, 1),
                   length = fmt(length_comp, 1), `age-length` = fmt(age_length, 1),
                   CPUE = fmt(cpue, 1), `max grad.` = sci(max_gradient),
                   `SB 1954` = fmt(sb_1954, 0), `SB 2022` = fmt(sb_2022, 0),
                   depletion = fmt(depletion, 3))], format = "pipe")

The diagnostic model was supplied with MFCL 2.2.7.0, which reproduces its objective function value exactly (M0). Each later step is refitted with the diagnostic model’s phase 9 settings (2200 evaluations), warm-started from the previous step; a fit takes 15-20 minutes. M1 and M3 stop at the evaluation limit with the line search stalled, at maximum gradients of a few times 10-6.

  • M1, no movement. The (fixed, SEAPODYM-derived) movement matrices are set to the identity, so the regions are closed populations. They still share the recruitment deviations (total recruitment split 0.819 / 0.181) and the stock-recruitment relationship, so the EPO data still inform region 1’s recruitment.
  • M1b, movement weeks on fishing dates. The movement weeks change from 37, 5, 17 and 29 (1 October and the first weeks of February, May and August) to 5, 17, 29 and 41 (February, May, August and November), all region 1 fishing dates. With no movement this changes nothing but MFCL’s time steps: it removes the extra period at the start of each year that MFCL adds at a movement week in a multi-region model, which a one-region model does not have (see the transplant check below), so that M1b-M2 changes only the regions. MFCL’s zero-fishing projection for M1b stops with a “sanity error” (the first period of a year is no longer a movement period), so M1b has no depletion; its fit converges.
  • M2, region 1 only. The EPO fisheries (14-17) and EPO index (20) are dropped and the region 1 indices renumbered 14 and 15. The par file is built from M1b’s: fishery- and region-indexed values are subset, region 1’s recruitment is kept by shifting the total population scaling parameter by log(0.818971), and the sections shaped by regions, movement or catch records come from MFCL’s -makepar for the one-region files (all zero or structural in this model). M2 removes the recruitment link to the EPO.
  • M3, growth fixed, no age-at-length. opal has no conditional age-at-length likelihood, so growth is fixed at M2’s estimates and the data dropped.
Code 
p1 = ggplot(TS, aes(year, sb / 1e3, colour = step)) + geom_line() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = step_col) + labs(x = NULL, y = "SB (kt)", colour = NULL)
p2 = ggplot(TS, aes(year, depletion, colour = step)) + geom_line() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = step_col) + labs(x = NULL, y = "SB / SB(F=0)", colour = NULL) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

Region 1’s spawning biomass in 1954 goes from 871 kt (M0) to 1,716, 3,413 and 6,594 kt, and depletion in 2022 from 0.50 to 0.75. In this catch-conditioned model the scale comes from the indices, the length compositions and their interaction with the catch; movement, the shared recruitment with the EPO and the age-at-length data each constrain it, and it drifts up as each is removed.

Code 
knitr::kable(bridge$transplant_check[, .(quantity, `vs M1` = sci(vs_m1, 1), `vs M1b` = sci(vs_m1b, 1))], format = "pipe")

With no movement, region 1 in M1 is unaffected by region 2’s catch or abundance (tested by setting region 2’s catch and recruitment near zero), and M2’s inputs match its region 1 exactly: every .frq record (catch, effort, CV and length frequencies) and every flag and parameter section of the par file, with the total population scaling parameter shifted by exactly log(0.818971). Recruitment, selectivity, growth, M and the predicted catches agree, but against M1 the numbers at the oldest ages drift up by a few percent and adult biomass by up to 1.3%.

The cause is in how MFCL builds its time steps. Each region’s year is split into periods at its fishing incidents and, in a multi-region model only, at the movement dates (check_for_missing_node() in rnaux2.cpp returns the movement nodes only if (num_regions > 1)). Natural mortality is shared equally among a year’s periods (fraction = -log(n)), not by elapsed time, and acts together with F in each period. MFCL’s year has 48 weeks (four per month); the movement weeks are calendar weeks, renumbered into the October-September model year like the records (get_history_data(), “renumber for month_1”). The diagnostic model’s weeks 37, 5, 17 and 29 are 1 October (the start of the model year) and the first weeks of February, May and August. Region 1 fishes in February, May and August but never in October, so M1’s region 1 has an extra period at the start of every year, which M2 (one region) does not. Moving the movement weeks onto fishing dates (M1b) removes the extra periods and the difference falls from 3.7% to 0.30% in numbers-at-age and from 1.3% to 0.15% in adult biomass. What is left is confined to the initial age structure (0.02% per age in 1954, gone by 1990), which MFCL builds from the average Z of the first ten periods, whose layout at the start of the series still differs. Removing regions therefore changes MFCL’s within-year timing of M as well as the data and the recruitment link; M1b separates that structural effect (M1-M1b) from the change of regions (M1b-M2).

4 Conversion to opal

shared/mfcl-to-opal/ reads MFCL’s .par, .frq, plot report and length.fit in base R and builds opal’s inputs (mfcl_to_opal()).

Code 
F = oc$fisheries
knitr::kable(F[, .(fishery, `MFCL diagnostic` = mfcl_diagnostic, name, `catch units` = units,
                   `catch total` = fmt(catch_total, 0), seasons = sel_seasons,
                   divisor = lf_divisor, quarters = lf_quarters, years = lf_years)], format = "pipe")
  • Time. MFCL’s model year starts in calendar month 10: the .frq dimension line’s ninth field (MFCL’s month_1), which the report gives as week 37. Calendar months 10-12 belong to the next model year (so the data’s last model year, 2022, has no calendar October-December). opal has 69 model years of four seasons (October-December, January-March, …), with recruitment and ageing at the start of the year. Fishing incidents in the same fishery and season are summed (troll catches are monthly).
  • Catch is in numbers for the longline fisheries and in tonnes for troll and driftnet; the two indices remove nothing.
  • Indices. MFCL’s survey likelihood is log-normal with variance λiσ2\lambda_i \sigma^2, where λi\lambda_i is the .frq CV column over its mean and σ\sigma fish flag 92 / 100 (0.2): opal’s standard errors are σλi\sigma \sqrt{\lambda_i}. Both indices are annual (longline in July-September, troll in January-March).
  • Length compositions. Samples below 50 fish are dropped, each is rescaled to its sample size capped at 1000, and they are summed by fishery and model year, with MFCL’s divisors as opal’s variance adjustments, under opal’s multinomial likelihood (MFCL: robust normal per incident).
  • Biology. Mean weight, maturity and M at age from MFCL’s report, so opal’s spawning biomass is MFCL’s adult biomass (numbers x weight x maturity at the start of the year). opal’s growth is used only for the length compositions: von Bertalanffy with age-specific K multipliers at ages 1-4 for MFCL’s independent mean lengths at ages 2-4 (RMSE 0.52 cm), SD linear in mean length between MFCL’s SDs at ages 1 and 12 (largest difference 0.47 cm).
  • Selectivity. MFCL’s selectivity-at-age, averaged over seasons weighted by each season’s catch (index fisheries: their survey season), as opal’s sel_fa_external.

5 opal at MFCL’s values

O0 holds everything at MFCL M3’s values. mfcl_match_recruitment() sets opal’s B0 from MFCL’s Beverton-Holt curve (R0=α−β/SPR0R_0 = \alpha - \beta / \text{SPR}_0, B0=R0SPR0B_0 = R_0 \text{SPR}_0), its initial deviations so that opal starts from MFCL’s 1954 numbers-at-age, and its recruitment deviations (bias adjustment off) so that it recruits MFCL’s recruitment every year.

Code 
knitr::kable(oc$o0_check[, .(quantity, `max rel. diff.` = sci(max_rel_diff, 1))], format = "pipe")

The replays are standalone simulations with MFCL’s estimates (not opal code). They cross catch removal at the start of each quarter, then a quarter of M (opal), or MFCL’s catch-conditioned Baranov in each fishing period (the year’s distinct incident dates, each with an equal share of the year’s M, as MFCL apportions it), with MFCL’s season-averaged selectivity (opal) or its seasonal selectivity.

Code 
knitr::kable(RP[, .(`rel. 2022` = pct(rel_mfcl[.N], 2), `max |rel.|` = pct(max(abs(rel_mfcl)), 2),
                    `max |rel.| vs O0` = pct(max(abs(sb / opal_o0 - 1)), 2)),
                by = .(timing, selectivity)], format = "pipe")

The opal-timing replay with averaged selectivity reproduces O0, which checks the replay. Catch timing accounts for almost all of the gap between O0 and MFCL; seasonal selectivity changes spawning biomass by less than 0.1%. The MFCL replay is within 0.5% of MFCL (0.6% with M shared by elapsed time instead); the remainder is largest in the mid-1990s, after the driftnet years, and may be the weight-at-age MFCL uses for catches in weight (not confirmed).

Code 
ggplot(RP, aes(year, rel_mfcl, colour = paste(timing, selectivity, sep = " / "))) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_line() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "SB relative to MFCL", colour = "timing / selectivity")

6 opal fits

O1 holds MFCL’s season-averaged selectivity, growth, steepness (0.8), sigmaR (0.64, MFCL’s CV of 0.71), M and the biology, and estimates B0, the recruitment deviations for 1955-2020 (the last two at the curve, as MFCL sets them at the mean), and the two index catchabilities. The initial population is unfished. O1 runs to the upper bound of log(B0) (22.00 against MFCL’s 14.04): spawning biomass in the billions of tonnes and depletion near 1.

Code 
pr = melt(PR[, .(log_B0, total = objective, cpue, `length comps` = lf, recruitment = rec)],
          id.vars = "log_B0")
pr[, delta := value - min(value), by = variable]
ggplot(pr, aes(log_B0, delta, colour = variable)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = lb_mfcl, linetype = 2) +
    labs(x = "log(B0)", y = "change in negative log-likelihood", colour = NULL)

Here and below, “MFCL’s scale” is MFCL’s Beverton-Holt B0 (log(B0) 14.04), the value O0 uses. The index and the recruitment penalty are best near it; the length compositions keep improving towards an unexploited stock and win.

7 Why the length compositions favour an unexploited stock

Code 
bf = lfd$by_fishery[variant == "annual"][order(change)]
knitr::kable(bf[, .(fishery, name, `n obs` = n_obs, `at MFCL` = fmt(at_mfcl, 1),
                    `at +3` = fmt(at_plus3, 1), change = fmt(change, 1))], format = "pipe")

The longline fisheries drive the pull; the troll fishery 11 prefers MFCL’s scale. With selectivity fixed, a lightly fished stock keeps more large, old fish, so opal’s predicted longline catches are too small for the data.

MFCL predicts each length sample at its date. Its length.fit gives, for each sample, the predicted composition by age, whose mean lengths show length-at-age growing through the model year (Figure 4); opal predicts every sample from start-of-year length-at-age.

Code 
lm_dt = data.table(month = rep(1:12, ncol(lfd$laa_month)), age = rep(seq_len(ncol(lfd$laa_month)), each = 12),
                   length = as.vector(lfd$laa_month))
ggplot(lm_dt[age <= 8], aes(month, length, colour = factor(age))) + geom_line() +
    geom_point(data = data.table(month = 1, age = 1:8, length = oc$growth$opal_length[1:8])) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
    labs(x = "model month", y = "mean length (cm)", colour = "age")

The test changes only opal’s inputs: its growth fitted to MFCL’s mid-year lengths (the average of model months 6 and 7). Figure 5 compares profiles over B0 for the annual model with start-of-year and mid-year growth, the same with fisheries 1-7 split into one fishery per season (Section 8), and the quarterly-age model.

Code 
pp = P[is.finite(objective)]
g1 = ggplot(pp, aes(dlog_B0, d_objective, colour = variant)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) + labs(x = "log(B0) - MFCL's", y = "change in objective", colour = NULL)
g2 = ggplot(pp, aes(dlog_B0, d_lf, colour = variant)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) + labs(x = "log(B0) - MFCL's", y = "change in length comps", colour = NULL)
g1 + g2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
Code 
knitr::kable(lfd$summary[, .(variant, `best log(B0) - MFCL's` = fmt(best_dlog_B0, 2),
                             `rise at +5` = fmt(rise_at_plus5, 1),
                             `depletion at MFCL's scale` = fmt(depletion_at_mfcl_scale, 3))], format = "pipe")

With mid-year growth the profile has a minimum near MFCL’s scale and the index fit improves, and O1-mid (O1 with mid-year growth, B0 estimated) converges at log(B0) 13.96 against MFCL’s 14.04. The length compositions on their own still favour a somewhat larger stock than MFCL’s.

7.1 Starting population

A B0 at MFCL’s does not give MFCL’s stock. MFCL scales its initial population with its own parameter (the total population scaling), separately from its stock-recruitment relationship, and its 1954 spawning biomass (6,594 kt) is about 5 times its Beverton-Holt B0, with 1954 recruitment 3.3 times its mean. O0 reproduces it only by imposing MFCL’s initial numbers (init_rdev_a); fitted opal models start from the unfished equilibrium at B0, as the assessment report describes but MFCL does not implement. O1-mid’s spawning biomass is 1,152 kt in 1954 and 425 kt in 2022, against MFCL’s 860 kt. Estimating the initial population, as MFCL does, closes most of the gap (O1i, Section 9).

The quarterly-age model, which gives each quarter MFCL’s length-at-age and selectivity and fits the length compositions by quarter, also has its minimum at MFCL’s scale and fits the indices far better than any annual variant (CPUE negative log-likelihood 0.71 at MFCL’s scale, against 15.73 for annual-mid and 44.66 for the O1 set-up). Its depletion at that B0 (0.467) is lower than the annual variants’, partly because its stock-recruitment curve is evaluated differently (Section 8); its B0 is not comparable with the annual models’ beyond being a scale.

Code 
g1 = ggplot(TR[model != "O1"], aes(year, sb / 1e3, colour = model)) + geom_line() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = model_col) + labs(x = NULL, y = "SB (kt)", colour = NULL)
g2 = ggplot(TR, aes(year, dynamic_depletion, colour = model)) + geom_line() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = model_col) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.05)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "SB / SB(F=0)", colour = NULL)
g1 + g2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

8 Seasonal set-ups

Both set-ups use opal’s inputs only.

Seasonal fisheries (mfcl_split_seasonal_fisheries()). Fisheries 1-7, whose MFCL selectivity differs by season, become four fisheries each (36 fisheries), each with one season’s catch, selectivity and length compositions. This represents MFCL’s seasonal selectivity exactly in the annual-age model and lets opal estimate seasonal curves; on its own it does not change the length-composition pull (Figure 5).

Quarterly ages (mfcl_quarterly_ages()). opal’s time step and age classes become quarters: 48 quarterly ages and 276 steps, one season each. Recruitment stays annual: the recruitment deviations of the three quarters without recruitment are fixed at -30, and the initial numbers of quarterly ages that do not exist (cohorts recruit once a year) are near zero. Then:

  • quarterly age q=4(a−1)+sq = 4(a - 1) + s holds annual age class aa in season ss only, so a selectivity by quarterly age is MFCL’s seasonal selectivity (exactly, except for the plus group, which is present in every season);
  • length-at-age, and weight at the time of catch, are MFCL’s at each quarter’s fishing month (opal’s growth fitted to them, RMSE 0.68 cm);
  • the length compositions are fitted by quarter, and the indices in the quarter they sample;
  • M is MFCL’s per quarter.
Code 
knitr::kable(lfd$o0q_check[, .(quantity, `rel. diff.` = sci(rel_diff, 1))], format = "pipe")

The cost is the stock-recruitment relationship: opal treats every step as a recruitment, so with one recruitment in four steps its B0 is about four times the unfished spawning biomass and the curve is evaluated at a quarter of the usual relative stock size, which changes what steepness means. Depletion has to be taken against opal’s unfished projection, and B0 treated as a scale parameter.

9 Fits with the quarterly ages and opal’s own selectivity

Five further fits (scripts/05-fit-opal-selectivity.r), with growth, steepness, sigmaR, M and the biology held as in O1. All estimate the initial population (Section 7.1): one deviation for the 1954 recruits (age 1) and one shared by the older ages, which sets the level of the initial age structure (in the quarterly models the plus group has its own), without the penalty against the stock-recruitment relationship (opal’s lambdas$init_rec = 0), as in MFCL.

  • O1i: O1-mid (annual, mid-year growth, MFCL’s selectivity) with the initial population estimated.
  • O1q: the quarterly-age model with MFCL’s seasonal selectivity fixed; B0, the first-quarter recruitment deviations (1955-2020), the initial population and the catchabilities estimated.
  • O2: the annual model with mid-year growth (O1-mid) and opal’s own length-based selectivity: double normals (a logistic for the longline index, which MFCL holds non-decreasing), shared within MFCL’s selectivity groups (fisheries 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 6). Three of the double normal’s six parameters are estimated: the peak and the two widths, within bounds (peak within 2 SD of the length bins, widths in [-6, 3]). The plateau and final selectivity are held at the starting curves’, which are fitted to MFCL’s selectivity-at-age through opal’s length-at-age, and the initial selectivity near zero. (A first attempt with five of the six free ran most widths, plateaus and final selectivities to their bounds.)
  • O2-split: O2 with fisheries 1-7 split into one fishery per season, sharing parameters within MFCL’s groups and seasons.
  • O2q: O1q with opal’s own selectivity (one curve per group, whose selectivity-at-age varies by quarter through growth).
Code 
SS = sel$summary
knitr::kable(SS[, .(model, `n par` = n_par, `max grad.` = sci(max_gradient), `at bound` = at_bound,
                    CPUE = fmt(cpue, 1), `length comps` = fmt(lf, 1),
                    `SB 2022` = fmt(sb_end / 1e3, 0), depletion = fmt(depletion_end, 3))], format = "pipe")
Code 
tr2 = rbind(TR[model %in% c("MFCL M3", "O1-mid"), .(model, year, sb)],
            sel$trajectory[model %in% c("O1i", "O1q", "O2", "O2q"), .(model, year, sb)])
ggplot(tr2, aes(year, sb / 1e3, colour = model)) + geom_line() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "SB (kt)", colour = NULL)
Code 
ff = c(3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14)
sel_dt = rbind(
  data.table(source = "MFCL", fishery = rep(ff, each = 12), age = rep(1:12, length(ff)),
             sel = as.vector(t(oc$selectivity$average[ff, ]))),
  data.table(source = "O2", fishery = rep(ff, each = 12), age = rep(1:12, length(ff)),
             sel = as.vector(t(sel$fits$O2$sel_fya[ff, ]))))
sel_dt[, name := oc$fishery_names[fishery]]
ggplot(sel_dt, aes(age, sel, colour = source)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~name) + labs(x = "age", y = "selectivity", colour = NULL)

With MFCL’s selectivity, estimating the initial population brings opal close to MFCL. O1i converges (largest gradient 1.1e-04) with 709 kt in 2022 and depletion 0.72, against MFCL’s 860 kt and 0.75. O1q (quarterly ages) agrees with it: the age-1 and older-age initial deviations are close to O1i’s and it ends at 695 kt. In the quarterly models the plus group shares the older ages’ initial level, with its equilibrium offset supplied through init_bias_adj_a (a fixed input; opal’s map cannot tie parameters with an offset); estimated on its own, it took the whole initial stock while the classes between went empty.

With opal’s selectivity the fits do not settle on sensible curves, even with three of the six parameters free. In O2 and O2q many double-normal widths go to their bounds (knife-edge limbs), the largest gradients stay above 1, and the stock is a quarter of MFCL’s in 2022. O2-split ends at a point where the gradient explodes as its curves collapse.

9.1 Why the double normals collapse

Code 
sdv = function(p, L) { m = sum(p * L) / sum(p); sqrt(sum(p * (L - m)^2) / sum(p)) }
spread = sdg$pooled[, .(obs_sd = sdv(observed, length), O1i_sd = sdv(O1i, length), O2_sd = sdv(O2, length)), by = fishery]
bf = merge(sdg$by_fishery, spread, by = "fishery")[order(-gain)]
knitr::kable(bf[, .(name, `n obs` = n_obs, `O1i NLL` = fmt(O1i_nll, 1), `O2 NLL` = fmt(O2_nll, 1),
                    `observed SD` = fmt(obs_sd, 1), `O1i SD` = fmt(O1i_sd, 1), `O2 SD` = fmt(O2_sd, 1))],
             format = "pipe")

O2 gains most on the troll fisheries 11 and 12 and the longline fishery 3, and loses on fishery 6. The northern longline fisheries’ (3, 4, 6, 7) and the longline index’s compositions are narrower (SD 5.8-7.4 cm) than the model predicts even with MFCL’s selectivity, and about as narrow as the spread of length within a single age at the ages they catch (MFCL’s SD of length is 5.9-7.6 cm at ages 5-12). Under the multinomial likelihood every tail bin counts, so opal narrows its predicted catch with a window-shaped selectivity in length: the knife-edge widths, which flatten selectivity-at-age over the older ages (Figure 8). MFCL’s robust normal likelihood is much less sensitive to the tails.

Code 
LT = lft$summary
knitr::kable(LT[, .(model, `max grad.` = sci(max_gradient), `widths at bound` = widths_at_bound,
                    CPUE = fmt(cpue, 1), `length comps` = fmt(lf, 1), `SD oldest age` = fmt(sd2, 2),
                    `SB 1954` = fmt(sb_1954 / 1e3, 0), `SB 2022` = fmt(sb_2022 / 1e3, 0),
                    depletion = fmt(depletion_2022, 3))], format = "pipe")

Pooling the tails changes little. The Dirichlet-multinomial’s dispersion goes to its upper bound (the multinomial) for most fisheries, since the sample sizes already carry MFCL’s Francis weights, except the longline index and the troll fisheries; the knife-edges remain. Estimating the SD of length at the oldest age matters: the compositions want 4.2-4.9 cm instead of MFCL’s 7.6, fewer widths reach their bounds, the index fit improves, and the scale changes from a quarter of MFCL’s to more than it. With all three (O2-all) the fit to both data types is the best and the stock is closest to MFCL’s (986 kt and 0.78 in 2022). The scale is therefore sensitive to the assumed spread of length at age, which MFCL fixes from its growth estimates with the age-at-length data. None of these fits is fully converged (largest gradients 0.25-1.4) and 10-19 widths still sit at bounds, so the selectivity remains to be constrained further (a width fixed, priors, or age-based curves) with the SD of length estimated.

9.2 Age-based and hybrid selectivity

scripts/08-fit-age-selectivity.r evaluates the double normals on age (opal’s sel_basis_f = 2) instead of on length through the length-at-age key, with the same three parameters free and the same groups; starting curves are fitted directly to MFCL’s selectivity-at-age. Growth then affects only the predicted length compositions.

  • O3: age-based curves for every fishery (the longline index logistic).
  • O3-SD2, O3-all: as O2-SD2 and O2-all.
  • O4: hybrid, with age-based curves for the longline fisheries and the index and length-based ones for the troll and driftnet fisheries (11, 12, 13, 15).
  • O4-all: O4 with tail pooling, the Dirichlet-multinomial and the SD of length at the oldest age estimated.
Code 
AS = asel$summary
knitr::kable(AS[, .(model, `max grad.` = sci(max_gradient), `widths at bound` = widths_at_bound,
                    CPUE = fmt(cpue, 1), `length comps` = fmt(lf, 1), `SD oldest age` = fmt(sd2, 2),
                    `SB 1954` = fmt(sb_1954 / 1e3, 0), `SB 2022` = fmt(sb_2022 / 1e3, 0),
                    depletion = fmt(depletion_2022, 3))], format = "pipe")
Code 
sa = asel$sel_age[model %in% c("MFCL", "O3", "O4") & fishery %in% c(3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14)]
ggplot(sa, aes(age, sel, colour = model)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~name) + labs(x = "age", y = "selectivity", colour = NULL)

Age-based curves keep MFCL’s domed shapes, with far fewer widths at their bounds, and fit every longline fishery’s compositions better than MFCL’s own selectivity does (O1i). They fail for the troll fisheries: these catch young fish (ages 1-4) whose lengths change quickly through the year, and a curve on whole ages cannot follow which lengths are caught in each season, so O3 loses about 1000 units on fishery 11 alone. The hybrid O4 keeps the age-based curves for the longline fisheries and length-based ones for troll and driftnet. It fits the compositions better than any other multinomial fit (O1i included), and its stock is the closest to MFCL’s: 886 kt and depletion 0.76 in 2022, against 860 kt and 0.75. It is not fully converged (largest gradient 1.0) and 7 widths are at bounds; with the SD of length estimated as well (O4-all) the gradient is smaller but the stock lower (591 kt).

9.2.1 Converging the hybrid, and its quarterly version

scripts/09-fit-hybrid-selectivity.r fixes each selectivity parameter that O4 left at a bound at that bound and refits the rest (O4-fix), and fits the hybrid on the quarterly-age model (O4q: age-based curves over the 48 quarterly ages for the longline fisheries and index, length-based for troll and driftnet, the initial population estimated with the plus group tied, started from O1q), then fixes its bounded parameters too (O4q-fix).

Code 
HY = hyb$summary
knitr::kable(HY[, .(model, `n par` = n_par, `max grad.` = sci(max_gradient), fixed = sel_fixed,
                    CPUE = fmt(cpue, 1), `length comps` = fmt(lf, 1),
                    `SB 1954` = fmt(sb_1954 / 1e3, 0), `SB 2022` = fmt(sb_2022 / 1e3, 0),
                    depletion = fmt(depletion_2022, 3))], format = "pipe")

Fixing the bounded parameters leaves the objectives unchanged and the fits converge: O4’s and O4q’s large gradients were only those of parameters pressing on their bounds. O4-fix (largest gradient 7.7e-04) keeps O4’s result, the closest to MFCL of the fits here. The quarterly hybrid O4q-fix also converges and fits both the indices and the quarterly compositions better than O1q, but its stock is about half O1q’s (359 kt and depletion 0.50 in 2022): on quarterly ages the age-based curves are smooth in age across the seasons, so they cannot follow MFCL’s seasonal selectivity the way a quarterly-age selectivity fixed at MFCL’s values (O1q) does, and the scale moves with them.

10 What opal would need

Code 
gaps = data.table(
  MFCL = c("Two regions with movement; recruitment distributed over regions",
           "Conditional age-at-length likelihood",
           "Length compositions predicted at each sample's date, with within-year growth",
           "Seasonal selectivity (fisheries 1-7)",
           "Catch-conditioned Baranov at each fishing incident's date (several per quarter for troll)",
           "Length-based cubic-spline selectivity, grouped across fisheries",
           "VB growth with independent mean lengths at ages 2-4; SD log-linear in length",
           "Length compositions per incident, robust normal likelihood",
           "Index abundance at the incident's date",
           "Recruitment from the previous year's spawning potential; last two at the mean",
           "Initial population scaled by its own parameter, apart from the stock-recruitment relationship"),
  opal = c("one region",
           "none",
           "start-of-year length-at-age; annual compositions",
           "selectivity by year",
           "Pope removal at the start of each season",
           "logistic, double normal, double Richards; no mirrors (sharing via map)",
           "VB, Richards, cessation, age-specific K; SD or CV linear in length",
           "annual compositions; multinomial, Dirichlet, Dirichlet-multinomial",
           "start of the season",
           "same year's spawning biomass; free deviations",
           "unfished (or init_F) equilibrium at B0, with optional initial deviations"),
  here = c("MFCL bridge to region 1 (M1, M2); scale doubles at each step",
           "dropped with growth fixed (M3); scale doubles",
           "the main cause of O1's unbounded scale; mid-year growth or quarterly ages fix it",
           "catch-weighted average; <0.1% on SB; seasonal fisheries or quarterly ages represent it",
           "up to ~2% on SB (O0 against the replays)",
           "MFCL's selectivity-at-age fixed (O0, O1)",
           "age-specific K at ages 1-4 (0.5 cm RMSE)",
           "summed by fishery and year; Francis divisors kept",
           "as opal (season-start numbers)",
           "MFCL's recruitment imposed (O0); last two deviations fixed (O1)",
           "MFCL's initial numbers imposed in O0; fits start lower (MFCL's 1954 SB is ~5x its B0)"))
knitr::kable(gaps, col.names = c("MFCL", "opal", "here"), format = "pipe")

In order of their effect on this stock: length-at-age at the time of sampling (or a sub-annual time step with annual recruitment, which would also give seasonal selectivity, catch weight and index timing), then catch timing within the season, then multiple regions, then a conditional age-at-length likelihood for estimating growth.

11 Reproducing this document

From any working directory (CLAUDE.md has the R environment):

Rscript --no-init-file case-studies/swpo-alb/scripts/01-build-mfcl-bridge.r
Rscript --no-init-file case-studies/swpo-alb/scripts/02-compare-mfcl-bridge.r
Rscript --no-init-file case-studies/swpo-alb/scripts/03-convert-fit-swpo-alb-opal.r
Rscript --no-init-file case-studies/swpo-alb/scripts/04-length-comp-diagnostics.r
quarto render case-studies/swpo-alb/vignettes/swpo-alb-mfcl-to-opal.qmd

The MFCL fits, opal fits and profiles are cached (SWPO_ALB_REFIT=true repeats them). The document reads only vignettes/data/.
